title: A Tibetan day

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bardo, and your line, in between. Did you notice one in-between moment and let it stay open? Day three hundred eighteen, the last day of the diamond vehicle.

Early morning in a Tibetan settlement in India. A grandmother wakes before her family, washes her face, and fills seven small bowls with water on the family shrine. She lights a lamp and bows three times. Then she walks out to the temple with her beads, joining a slow river of people circling it clockwise, murmuring, turning the prayer wheels as they pass. Later she'll sit for a while at home. None of it is dramatic. All of it has a shape. Today: a Tibetan day.
screen: `SEVEN BOWLS OF WATER.` → `A LAMP, THREE BOWS.` → `CIRCLING THE TEMPLE WITH BEADS.`

segments.voice: Tibetan teachers often say a practice should be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end. Here's how that looks. It begins with refuge: turning toward the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and in Tibetan practice often the teacher too. Right after comes bodhicitta: the reminder of why, for all beings. Many people say a short traditional verse joining the two, three times. That's the beginning. The middle is the practice itself. It might be om mani padme hum on the beads, or a praise to Tara, or a visualization, or tonglen, riding the breath. Whatever it is, teachers say to do it without grabbing at results. And the end is dedication. Whatever good came from this, it's given away, to all beings, so it can't turn into a private trophy. A session of ten minutes and a retreat of three years share that same shape. Around it sits the rest of the day: water bowls and lamps, the walk around the temple, the wheels, the flags on the roof. Now look back at two weeks on the roof of the world. The diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. Turn the mind. Check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. Four streams. Carried into exile. In between. And today, the diamond day. Tomorrow the path comes down from the mountains, to wherever you live, and asks a practical question: who will you practice with?
screen: `BEGINNING: REFUGE AND BODHICITTA.` · `MIDDLE: MANTRA, TARA, TONGLEN.` · `END: GIVE THE GOOD AWAY.` · `WATER BOWLS, LAMPS, THE TEMPLE WALK.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape in miniature. For the beginning, turn your attention, silently, toward what you take refuge in, and remember why you're sitting: not only for yourself. For the middle, sit with the breath, or murmur om mani padme hum if that feels right, without chasing any result. For the end, when the bell rings, give it away: whatever good came from this, for all beings. Another day, you can stretch this shape to fifteen minutes. The bell holds the time.
A Tibetan day. Refuge and bodhicitta at the start, mantra or tonglen in the middle, and dedication at the end: good in the beginning, middle and end.
Your line: the diamond day. Give today a beginning, a middle and an end: a moment of why this morning, care in the middle, and tonight, give the good away. Day three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often begin the day with water-bowl offerings and prostrations, circle temples and stupas clockwise with prayer beads, and shape each practice session with refuge and bodhicitta at the start and a dedication of merit at the end.

fork.setup: you've just finished a good sit and feel great. a Tibetan teacher would say there's one more step. what is it?
options: write down how good it felt.
dedicate whatever good came from it to all beings.

fork.reveal: the session ends with dedication: the good is given away to all beings, which completes the shape.

original.note: Sanskrit pariṇāmanā: dedication, turning the merit of practice toward the good of all beings. Tibetan: ngowa.

trapdoor: what you thought: Tibetan practice is mostly exotic ritual.
what it means: a simple shape: refuge and bodhicitta, practice without grabbing, dedication.
what a scholar hears: the 'three excellences' (good motivation, non-conceptual practice, dedication) frame sessions in all four Tibetan schools.
